en: The Sūtra on the Elder Mahāpuṣpa Asking the Buddha about the Nārāyaṇa Power.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra together with Liyan.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the country of Śrāvastī at the Jetavana...
In the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
the elder Mahāpuṣpamaṇḍala rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
“Venerable World-Honored One!
"What reward shall one obtain who gives food and drink to all sentient beings?
At that time, the Bhagavān said to the elder:
"One who gives food obtains the power of a Tathāgata."
Then the great householder again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps a simile by which the power of the Tathāgata might be proclaimed, so that I may hear it?”
The Buddha addressed the householder, saying:
"There is, son of good family!
It cannot be explained by means of few causes and conditions."
He further addressed the householder:
"The strength of ten ordinary oxen is equal to the strength of one hump-backed ox; the strength of ten hump-backed oxen is equal to the strength of one rhinoceros;
the strength of ten rhinoceroses is equal to the strength of one ordinary elephant; and the strength of ten ordinary elephants is equal to the strength of one *śārdūla* [wild buffalo]."
The *bala* is shaped like a deer, with a face resembling that of a rhinoceros and a body possessing eight legs—four on its back and four planted on the ground for locomotion.
When it tires from walking, it turns over onto its back to rest; it then places its upper legs downward to tread upon the earth as it moves.
Its strength is capable of carrying an elephant; ten *śalabha* strengths are equal to the strength of one *yuddhagaja* (battle-elephant), and ten [of those]...
The strength of a fighting elephant is equal to the strength of one intoxicated elephant; ten times the strength of an intoxicated elephant is equal to the strength of one wild elephant;
ten times the strength of a wild elephant is equal to the strength of one *kalabha* elephant;
ten times the strength of a *kalabha* elephant is equal to the strength of one *kumuda* elephant; ten times the strength of a *kumuda* elephant is equal to the strength of one *utpala* elephant.
The strength of ten *ro-ma* elephants equals the strength of one *utpala* elephant; the strength of ten *utpala* elephants equals the strength of one *nīlotpala* elephant;
the strength of ten *nīlotpala* elephants equals the strength of one great fragrant elephant (*mahāgandhahastin*);
the strength of ten great fragrant elephants equals the strength of one five-colored lion king; and the strength of ten lion kings equals the strength of one man among the champions (*malla*).
As for strength: ten times the strength of a common strongman equals the strength of one *nī-kūla*;
ten times the strength of a *nī-kūla* equals the strength of one *aṭṭhuna*; ten times the strength of an *aṭṭhuna* equals the strength of one *vimasena*;
ten times the strength of a *vimasena* equals the strength of one *nārāyaṇa*. Six hundred and sixty-three *nārāyaṇa*s [equal the strength of the Buddha].
Equal to the power of a single pore of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
each and every one of his eighty-four thousand pores possesses such Nārāyaṇa strength; the power of these eighty-four thousand pores is equal to the power of a single joint of the Bhagavat.
The Buddha told the householder:
"By this you should know that within each and every joint of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, there are fully eighty-four thousand six hundred and sixty-three kinds of Nārāyaṇa strength."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the elder Mahāpuṣpamaṇḍita, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
This concludes the Sutra on the Nārāyaṇa Power asked by the Elder Mahāpuṣpamaṇḍita.
